_comment: CN-COMPONENTS (constitution §22, D-068): metadata for the accessible component library. The 3 'ready' entries have a real, working, keyboard-accessible implementation in src/components/library/<impl>.tsx, rendered live on their page; their displayed code is that file's real source (Vite ?raw import). 'planned' entries are named honestly on the index with no page and no broken link. Invariants (required fields, ready→impl file exists, ready slugs mirrored in sitemap + audit gate) are enforced by scripts/components.test.mjs. Nothing here is invented: keyboard/SR/ARIA facts follow the WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices patterns and the shipped implementations.

components.name: Accordion
components.summary: Stacked sections that expand and collapse independently. The foundational aria-expanded disclosure pattern that a dozen other widgets build on.

keyboard.does: toggles the focused section open or closed
moves between section headers and into an open panel

screenReader: Each header is announced as a button carrying its state — “collapsed” or “expanded”.
Toggling re-announces the new state; the revealed panel is exposed as a region labelled by its header.
Because the headers are real headings, heading navigation still lists every section.
ariaNotes: The trigger is a native <button> inside a heading (h2–h4), so role, focus and Enter/Space come from the platform.
aria-expanded on the button reflects the panel state; aria-controls links the button to its panel id.
A collapsed panel is removed from the DOM entirely, so nothing hidden is focusable or read out.

pitfalls.bad: A <div> with onClick as the header.
pitfalls.good: Use a real <button> so keyboard, focus and role are free and correct.

pitfalls.bad: The collapsed panel is only visually hidden but stays in the tab order.
pitfalls.good: Remove it from the DOM (or use the hidden attribute) so it is not reachable.

pitfalls.bad: No aria-expanded, so a screen reader cannot tell open from closed.
pitfalls.good: Toggle aria-expanded on the button on every state change.

components.name: Tabs
components.summary: One panel visible at a time, chosen from a row of tabs. Teaches the roving-tabindex idea and arrow-key navigation that trip up most hand-rolled versions.

keyboard.does: moves to the previous / next tab and selects it, wrapping at the ends
moves to the first / last tab
leaves the tablist and moves into the selected panel

screenReader: The tablist is announced with its accessible name; each tab reports whether it is selected and its position (“2 of 3”).
Arrowing to another tab re-announces it; the shown panel is labelled by its tab.
ariaNotes: Roving tabindex: only the selected tab has tabindex 0, the rest tabindex -1, so Tab does not walk through every tab.
role=“tab” + aria-selected on each tab; role=“tabpanel” + aria-labelledby on each panel; aria-controls links them.
Hidden panels use the hidden attribute, removing them from both the tab order and the accessibility tree.

pitfalls.bad: Every tab is a tab stop, so Tab cycles through all of them before reaching the panel.
pitfalls.good: Use a roving tabindex; the arrow keys move between tabs instead.

pitfalls.bad: The arrow keys do nothing.
pitfalls.good: Handle Left / Right / Home / End on the tablist.

pitfalls.bad: Automatic activation on a panel that is expensive to render, so arrowing lags.
pitfalls.good: For heavy panels use manual activation — arrows move focus, Enter/Space selects.

components.name: Modal dialog
components.pattern: Dialog · focus trap + Escape + focus return
components.summary: A dialog that takes over the page until dismissed. The pattern where a broken implementation strands keyboard users most visibly — focus trap, Escape, and returning focus are all things static markup cannot promise.

keyboard.does: cycles through the focusable elements inside the dialog only — focus is trapped
closes the dialog

screenReader: On open, focus moves into the dialog and its accessible name (the title) is announced.
aria-modal=“true” tells the screen reader to treat everything outside the dialog as unavailable.
ariaNotes: role=“dialog” with aria-modal=“true” and aria-labelledby pointing at the visible title.
Focus is moved into the dialog on open and returned to the triggering element on every close path.
Focus is trapped: Tab and Shift+Tab wrap within the dialog and never reach the page behind it.

pitfalls.bad: Focus stays on the page behind the dialog, so Tab walks into hidden content.
pitfalls.good: Move focus into the dialog on open and trap it there.

pitfalls.bad: Closing the dialog drops focus to the top of the page.
pitfalls.good: Return focus to the element that opened the dialog.

pitfalls.bad: No Escape handler — the dialog can only be closed with the mouse.
pitfalls.good: Close on Escape as well as the close button.

pitfalls.bad: aria-modal=“true” with no real focus constraint.
pitfalls.good: aria-modal is a promise to assistive tech — back it with an actual focus trap.

components.name: Tooltip
components.pattern: Tooltip · role=tooltip, aria-describedby, Escape to dismiss
components.summary: A supplementary label revealed on hover and focus, dismissible with Escape, never the only place critical information lives. The pattern where showing it on hover alone is the single most common way tooltips break for keyboard users.

keyboard.does: moves focus to the trigger, which shows the tooltip — the primary way keyboard users see it
hides the tooltip; focus stays on the trigger, it is never moved

screenReader: The trigger is announced as normal (its own role and name), followed by its description — the tooltip text — because the trigger's aria-describedby points at it.

Nothing is announced as a separate interruption: a description is read as part of the trigger, not as a live announcement, so this pattern is silent for anyone who is not currently focused on the trigger.
Moving focus away hides the tooltip and removes the description association until the trigger is focused again.
ariaNotes: role="tooltip" on the bubble; the trigger carries aria-describedby pointing at its id — describedby, not labelledby, because a tooltip supplements the trigger's existing accessible name, it does not replace it.
aria-describedby is added only while the tooltip is visible and removed when it hides, so a screen reader is never pointed at an id that is not currently meaningful.
The trigger shows the tooltip on both focus and hover — hover alone is not sufficient, because it is entirely invisible to anyone who never moves a mouse.

WCAG 1.4.13 (Content on Hover or Focus): the tooltip is dismissible (Escape, without moving focus), hoverable (the pointer can move from the trigger onto the tooltip itself without it disappearing — a short grace period on mouseleave allows that), and persistent (it does not vanish on its own timer while still hovered or focused).

pitfalls.bad: The tooltip only shows on mouseover/mouseout.
pitfalls.good: Show it on focus as well as hover — otherwise a keyboard user never sees it at all.

pitfalls.bad: Escape (or any dismissal) moves focus off the trigger.
pitfalls.good: Dismiss the tooltip only; leave focus exactly where it was.

pitfalls.bad: aria-labelledby is used to attach the tooltip.
pitfalls.good: Use aria-describedby — a tooltip supplements the accessible name, it is not the name itself.

pitfalls.bad: A tooltip contains a link or a button so it can be "more useful".
pitfalls.good: Tooltips cannot safely contain interactive content — if you need that, the correct pattern is a popover (a dialog-like disclosure), not a tooltip.

pitfalls.bad: Moving the pointer toward the tooltip to read more of it makes the tooltip disappear first.
pitfalls.good: Give the pointer a short grace period to reach the tooltip, and keep it open while the pointer is over the tooltip itself (WCAG 1.4.13 hoverable).

components.name: Combobox
components.summary: A text input paired with a filterable listbox popup — the most intricate composite widget, and the one autocomplete UIs most often break. The pattern where the highlighted option is not really focused: DOM focus stays in the text field the whole time, and aria-activedescendant is what tells a screen reader where you are.

keyboard.does: filters the list to options containing what you typed (case-insensitive) and opens the popup if it was closed
moves the active option and wraps at both ends; opens the popup first if it was closed. The caret never leaves the text field
opens the popup without activating an option — “show me the list, I am not choosing yet”
jumps to the first / last option currently visible while the popup is open; with the popup closed they keep their normal meaning and move the caret
selects the active option, puts its label in the field and closes the popup; focus stays in the field. With the popup open it never submits the surrounding form
closes the popup without selecting; what you typed and where your focus is both stay exactly as they were
leaves the field, which closes the popup without selecting

screenReader: The field is announced by its label and as a combobox, with its expanded state — so the user knows a list can open before they open it.

Arrowing through the list announces each option (“Germany, 12 of 19”) even though nothing was actually focused: the input's aria-activedescendant points at the active option, and the screen reader follows that pointer.
Because real focus never leaves the input, the user can keep typing to narrow the list at any point without first returning from the list — the two actions do not compete.
A filter with no results is announced through a role="status" line inside the popup, so the user hears “No matches for …” instead of silence and an empty box.
Selecting closes the popup and the field now reads back the chosen label, which is the confirmation that the choice landed.
ariaNotes: role="combobox" goes on the text input itself (ARIA 1.2), together with aria-expanded, aria-haspopup="listbox", aria-controls pointing at the popup, and aria-autocomplete="list" — list, because the popup filters and the field is never rewritten behind the user.

aria-activedescendant on the input carries the id of the active option; the options themselves are NOT focusable and carry no tabindex. This is the opposite of the roving-tabindex arrangement used by tabs, and it is what allows an editable field to keep receiving keystrokes while the user walks the list.

The visual highlight is styling only (a data attribute here). Styling without aria-activedescendant leaves a screen-reader user moving through a list silently; aria-activedescendant without a visible highlight leaves a sighted keyboard user with no idea where they are. Both are required.
Each option is role="option" with a unique id and aria-selected; aria-selected marks the active option, and the committed value is shown by the field itself.
aria-controls is set only while the popup exists — a relationship pointing at an id that has been removed is a broken relationship, not a harmless leftover.
Nothing is auto-activated by typing, so aria-activedescendant is absent until the user arrows into the list: Enter then can only commit an option the user actually moved to.

pitfalls.bad: The arrow keys call option.focus(), moving real DOM focus onto the list.
pitfalls.good: Keep focus in the input and move aria-activedescendant instead — otherwise typing stops working the moment the user presses Down.

pitfalls.bad: The active option is only highlighted with CSS.
pitfalls.good: Pair the highlight with aria-activedescendant on the input, so the option is announced as well as drawn.

pitfalls.bad: The popup closes on blur, so clicking an option never selects it — mousedown blurs the field before click fires.
pitfalls.good: preventDefault() on the option's mousedown: focus stays in the field and the click lands.

pitfalls.bad: The native input keeps its browser autofill (autoComplete left at the default).
pitfalls.good: Set autocomplete="off" — otherwise the browser's own dropdown covers the popup and answers the same arrow keys.

pitfalls.bad: Escape clears the field, or moves focus somewhere else.
pitfalls.good: Escape dismisses the popup only; the typed text and the focus position both survive.

pitfalls.bad: An empty filter shows an empty listbox, or a fake “No results” option.
pitfalls.good: Show a real message in a role="status" line — a fake option is announced as “option 1 of 1” and can be selected as a value.

pitfalls.bad: The active option is scrolled out of the popup's viewport.
pitfalls.good: Scroll it into view yourself — nothing is really focused, so the browser will not do it for you.

components.name: Menu button
components.summary: A button that opens a menu of actions, navigable with the arrow keys and closable with Escape. The pattern where the highlighted item is only a CSS state: real DOM focus moves onto the menu items themselves (roving tabindex), the opposite arrangement from this library's Combobox.

keyboard.keys: Enter / Space / Down / Up (on the button)
keyboard.does: opens the menu; Down puts focus on the first item, Up puts focus on the last item — the same convention as native OS menus
moves real focus to the next/previous item and wraps at both ends
moves focus to the first / last item
moves focus to the next item whose label starts with that letter, cyclically — a single keystroke, not a buffered filter
runs that item, closes the menu, and returns focus to the button
closes the menu without running anything and returns focus to the button
closes the menu and moves on to the next element in the page's tab order — focus is not pulled back to the button, because Tab is a "move to what's next" key, not a dismiss key

screenReader: The button is announced with its expanded state and that it has a popup menu (aria-haspopup="menu"), before the user opens it.

Opening the menu moves real focus onto the first (or, via Up, the last) item, so it is announced as a menu item, its position in the menu, and the menu's own accessible name — the same experience a screen-reader user gets from any other focusable control, because it genuinely is one here.
Each further arrow/Home/End/type-ahead move re-announces the newly focused item; nothing is announced as a pointer moving over a highlight.
Escape and Tab are both silent on the way out (no extra announcement) beyond whatever the newly focused element itself announces — the button on Escape, the next tabbable element on Tab.
ariaNotes: The trigger is a real <button> with aria-haspopup="menu", aria-expanded reflecting the live open/closed state, and aria-controls pointing at the menu's id only while it exists.

The container is role="menu" with aria-label naming it; each action is role="menuitem". This library keeps every item a plain action (no checkbox/radio menuitem variants) — the pattern's simplest, most common shape.

Roving tabindex: exactly one item carries tabindex=0 (the one that would receive focus next) and every other item carries tabindex=-1. Moving between items calls a real .focus() on the target element via a ref — this is the same mechanism as this library's Tabs, not the aria-activedescendant virtual focus used by Combobox. A menu's items are not editable text, so nothing needs to keep the caret parked elsewhere the way Combobox's input does — real focus is the simpler, correct default here.

aria-controls is set only while the menu is open, matching Combobox and Breadcrumbs' other conditional relationships in this library — an id reference to something that no longer exists is a broken relationship, not a harmless leftover.

pitfalls.bad: The highlighted item is only a CSS class; DOM focus stays on the button the whole time it is open.
pitfalls.good: Move real focus onto the active menu item (roving tabindex) — a screen-reader user arrowing through the menu must hear each item as it becomes current, not just see a highlight move.

pitfalls.bad: Escape or Enter closes the menu but leaves focus on whatever item happened to be active, or drops it to the top of the page.
pitfalls.good: Return focus to the button on every keyboard close path (Escape, and Enter/Space after running an item) — the button is where the interaction started.

pitfalls.bad: Tab is intercepted to force focus back onto the button, the same as Escape.
pitfalls.good: Let Tab close the menu and continue moving through the page's own tab order — APG treats Tab as "move to what's next", not a dismiss key, and hijacking it fights the browser.

pitfalls.bad: Up on the closed button opens the menu at the first item, same as Down.
pitfalls.good: Up opens at the LAST item — the native-menu convention for "I'm approaching from the bottom".

pitfalls.bad: Typing a letter filters the menu down to matching items, like a combobox.
pitfalls.good: A menu's type-ahead is a single-keystroke jump to the next matching item, cyclically — not a buffered filter; menus don't narrow their own contents.

pitfalls.bad: A click outside the menu is ignored, or the menu is closed by making the button re-steal focus from whatever the user just clicked.
pitfalls.good: Close without activating anything and without moving focus — the user's click already told the browser where they wanted to be.

components.name: Select (listbox)
components.summary: A collapsible single-select listbox: a button that opens a popup role="listbox" for cases where the native <select> cannot be styled to requirements — the native element stays the honest first choice everywhere else.

keyboard.keys: Enter / Space / Down / Up (on the button)
keyboard.does: opens the popup; focus lands on the currently selected option, or the first option if nothing is selected yet
moves real focus to the next/previous option and wraps at both ends — the selection is not changed yet
moves focus to the first / last option
moves focus to the next option whose label starts with that letter, cyclically — a single keystroke, not a buffered filter
confirms the focused option as the selection, closes the popup, and returns focus to the button
closes the popup WITHOUT changing the selection and returns focus to the button

screenReader: The button is announced with the field's label, its own current value or placeholder, and that it has a popup listbox (aria-haspopup="listbox") with its expanded state, before the user opens it.

Opening the popup moves real focus onto the currently selected option (or the first option), so it is announced as an option, its position and selected state in the list, and the listbox's own accessible name — the same experience a screen-reader user gets from any other focusable control, because it genuinely is one here.

Each further arrow/Home/End/type-ahead move re-announces the newly focused option; nothing is announced as a pointer moving over a highlight, and moving focus alone does not announce a new selection because moving focus alone does not select anything.
Confirming an option (Enter/Space/click) moves focus back to the button, which now announces the newly selected value as part of its own accessible name.
ariaNotes: The trigger is a real <button> with aria-haspopup="listbox", aria-expanded reflecting the live open/closed state, aria-controls pointing at the popup's id only while it exists, and aria-labelledby joining the field's label with the button's own visible text (the ARIA APG collapsible-listbox two-id pattern) so the announced name always includes the current value or an honest placeholder — never a bare "button".

The popup is role="listbox" with aria-labelledby naming it from the same field label; each item is role="option" with aria-selected on the one committed value — not on whatever option merely has focus while the user is still arrowing through the list.

Roving tabindex: exactly one option carries tabindex=0 (the one that would receive focus next) and every other option carries tabindex=-1. Moving between options calls a real .focus() on the target element via a ref — the same mechanism as this library's Tabs and Menu button, not the aria-activedescendant virtual focus Combobox uses. Nothing inside this popup is editable text, so nothing needs to keep a caret parked elsewhere the way Combobox's input does — real focus is the simpler, correct default here, the same reasoning Menu button already gives for its own items.

Selection intentionally does not follow focus: a separate 'focused option' and 'selected option' let Escape close the popup by touching nothing, instead of reverting a value that arrow keys had already overwritten — APG allows either model for a single-select listbox, and this one is the one that makes Escape's 'change nothing' promise literally true rather than an emulated undo.

pitfalls.bad: The button's visible label is empty or reads a raw value like the internal slug when nothing is selected yet.
pitfalls.good: Show an honest placeholder (e.g. "Select a standard…") until a real option is chosen, and the option's human label afterwards — never a blank control a screen reader announces as nothing.

pitfalls.bad: Arrowing through options immediately overwrites the committed selection (selection follows focus), so Escape can only fake a revert by remembering the value the popup had on open.
pitfalls.good: Keep focus and selection as two different pieces of state: arrow keys move focus only, Enter/Space commits it, and Escape closes without touching the committed value at all.

pitfalls.bad: Opening the popup always starts at the first option, even when a value is already selected.
pitfalls.good: Open with focus on the currently selected option (falling back to the first option only when nothing is selected) — losing your place every time you reopen a long list is the most common native-<select>-replacement complaint.

pitfalls.bad: The highlighted option is only a CSS class; DOM focus stays on the button the whole time the popup is open.
pitfalls.good: Move real focus onto the focused option (roving tabindex), the same mechanism this library's Menu button uses — a screen-reader user arrowing through the list must hear each option as it becomes current, not just see a highlight move.

pitfalls.bad: Typing a letter filters the option list down to matches, like a combobox.
pitfalls.good: A listbox popup's type-ahead is a single-keystroke jump to the next matching option, cyclically — not a buffered filter; the full option list stays present the whole time.

components.name: Breadcrumbs
components.summary: An ordered trail of ancestor links inside a named nav landmark, with the current page marked by aria-current and left unlinked. The pattern where typing the separator into the markup quietly makes every level noisier to listen to.

keyboard.does: moves through the ancestor links; the current page is not a link and is skipped, because there is nowhere to go

screenReader: The landmark is announced by its label — “Breadcrumb navigation” — which is why the aria-label matters on a page that also has a main nav, and why a second trail on the same page needs a different name.
The list announces its length, so the user knows how deep the trail is before moving through it.
The separators are CSS ::after content and are never announced; a “/” typed into the markup would be read aloud between every item.
The last item is announced as the current page thanks to aria-current=“page”.
ariaNotes: nav needs aria-label (or aria-labelledby) whenever the page carries more than one navigation landmark — and the name must be unique among them, which is why the label here is a prop and not a constant.
aria-current=“page” belongs on the item representing the page you are on — not on an ancestor, and not on every item.
An <ol>, not a <ul>: the order of a trail is meaningful.

pitfalls.bad:
Writing the separator as text:
  • Home
    • /
  • Countries
    • .
pitfalls.good: Draw it with CSS ::after — decoration must not reach the accessibility tree.

pitfalls.bad: Linking the current page to itself and leaving it unmarked.
pitfalls.good: Render it as plain text carrying aria-current=“page”.

pitfalls.bad: Two nav landmarks sharing one name — a hard-coded aria-label="Breadcrumb" beside the site's own trail.
pitfalls.good: Name each landmark distinctly; axe's landmark-unique catches the collision, and without it a screen-reader user cannot tell the two apart.

components.name: Pagination
components.summary: Page-by-page navigation of a long list, with the current page marked and controls that read clearly out of context.

components.name: Toast / status message
components.summary: A transient notification announced through a polite or assertive live region without stealing focus. The ARIA live-region pattern, where the hard part is invisible: the region has to exist before the message does.

keyboard.does: reaches each visible toast's Dismiss button — toasts do not steal focus, so they sit in the normal tab order
on a focused Dismiss button, removes that toast

screenReader: A polite status (“Changes saved”) is announced at the next natural pause, without interrupting whatever is currently being read.
An error is announced immediately as an alert, interrupting the current speech because it needs attention now.
Focus never moves to the toast — the user stays exactly where they were, and the message simply arrives in the background.
ariaNotes: The live region is rendered from first paint — empty — so assistive tech is already observing it when a message is inserted. A region that mounts together with its first message is frequently not announced at all.
role="status" carries an implicit aria-live="polite"; role="alert" an implicit aria-live="assertive". Match the politeness to the urgency — assertive is only for things that must interrupt.
aria-atomic="false" so only the newly added toast is announced, not the whole stack re-read on every change.

pitfalls.bad: The toast element is added to the DOM only when the first message fires.
pitfalls.good: Render the empty live region up front and insert only the message text into it — otherwise the very first toast is silent.

pitfalls.bad: Everything uses role="alert", so a routine “saved” message rudely interrupts the screen reader.
pitfalls.good: Use role="status" (polite) for success and info; reserve role="alert" (assertive) for errors.

pitfalls.bad: Focus is moved onto the toast so it “gets noticed”.
pitfalls.good: Leave focus where it is — a live region announces without stealing focus, which is the entire point of the pattern.

pitfalls.bad: An error toast auto-dismisses after three seconds, before a screen-reader user can read or act on it.
pitfalls.good: Let errors persist until dismissed; only auto-clear low-stakes polite messages (WCAG 2.2.1, Timing Adjustable).

components.name: Switch
components.summary: An on/off toggle distinct from a checkbox, reporting its state as “on” or “off”.

components.name: Data table
components.summary: A sortable, semantic table with proper header association and aria-sort, readable cell by cell.

components.name: Form field
components.summary: A labelled input with programmatically associated help and error messages, and errors announced without a focus jump.

keyboard.does: moves focus onto the control itself — the label is not a separate stop, only the wrapped field is
behaves exactly as the wrapped native control would on its own; the wrapper adds no keyboard behaviour of its own

screenReader: The label is announced as the field's accessible name because <label htmlFor> targets the control's id directly — visual proximity in the markup is not what creates that association.
The hint is read as part of the field's description as soon as it exists, before any error is present.

When an error appears, it is announced immediately as an alert; it does not replace the hint in the field's description — both ids stay joined in aria-describedby, so the next time the field is described (e.g. re-focused), both are read.
aria-invalid is announced as an invalid entry only while a real error exists; it disappears — not "becomes false" — the moment the error clears.
ariaNotes: label uses htmlFor pointing at the control's id, not implicit wrapping — the association keeps working for control types that don't nest cleanly inside a <label>.

aria-describedby is the union of the hint id and the error id, joined by a space, never one replacing the other — the most common way real forms break this pattern is losing the hint's aria-describedby the instant the error's takes over, exactly when the hint is needed most.

aria-invalid is set to true only when an error is actually present; it is omitted the rest of the time, not hardcoded to "false" — an explicit false is itself noise some screen readers announce, and it erases the one moment the attribute matters.
The error text lives in role="alert", so it is announced without moving focus off the field the user is still typing into.

pitfalls.bad: The hint's id is dropped from aria-describedby the moment an error appears.
pitfalls.good: Join both ids — [hintId, errorId].filter(Boolean).join(' ') — so the hint stays available exactly when the user needs it most.

pitfalls.bad: aria-invalid="false" is hardcoded on every field, error or not.
pitfalls.good: Omit aria-invalid entirely until there is a real error — an explicit "false" is noise, and it hides the one moment the attribute is meaningful.

pitfalls.bad: The error message exists in the DOM but nothing points a screen reader at it.
pitfalls.good: Give it an id inside aria-describedby (and role="alert", as here) — text that only sits visually near the field is invisible to anyone not looking at the screen.

pitfalls.bad: Focus is moved to the error message, or to the top of the form, when validation fails.
pitfalls.good: Leave focus exactly where it was — the field the user is already in — and let role="alert" announce the error in the background.

pitfalls.bad: A label element sits visually above the input with no htmlFor and no id on the input to match it.
pitfalls.good: Use <label htmlFor={id}> with a matching id on the control, so screen readers announce the name programmatically, not just sighted users seeing it nearby.
